argv:
Rewrite the text following the Microsoft writing style.

Sound like a helpful colleague chatting with the reader, not a manual. Use
contractions everywhere they'd naturally occur, address the reader directly as
"you", and reach for everyday words over formal ones. A sentence fragment is
fine when it lands the point — don't force every thought into a full clause.

Open with the single thing the reader most needs to know, then explain. Keep
sentences short and let the page's shape (headings, short paragraphs) do some
of the work.

Use sentence case for any heading. Use the active voice and the present tense.
Tell the reader exactly what to do and what happens next, in a tone that feels
like a quick conversation rather than a document.

Skip jargon, hedging, and anything that talks down to the reader — but don't
skip the personality. A little warmth and a casual aside are welcome.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
A generation begins with three files: a style guide, a corpus passage, and a
prompt template. The runner parses the frontmatter of each, hashes the file
whole, and records the hash alongside the output. The guide's body becomes the
system prompt. The passage is substituted into the template to form the user
prompt, which is written to the child process on standard input rather than
passed as an argument, so that no shell quoting rule and no command-line length
limit ever applies to it. The runner then spawns the Claude Code CLI with an
explicit argument vector, requests a JSON envelope, and waits with a timeout
that escalates from a polite termination signal to a forced kill. What comes
back is parsed even when the process exits non-zero, because a refusal arrives
that way: a failing exit code and a well-formed envelope that names the reason.
Every field of that envelope is written to disk, successful or not, along with
the argument vector, the resolved model, the token counts, and the wall-clock
duration.
</passage>

response.text:
Here's what kicks off every generation: a style guide, a corpus passage, and a prompt template. The runner reads the frontmatter from each one, hashes the whole file, and saves that hash right next to the output. Simple as that.

The guide's body becomes your system prompt. The passage drops into the template to form the user prompt — and that prompt goes to the child process over standard input, not as a command-line argument. Why? So you never have to worry about shell quoting or length limits messing things up.

From there, the runner spawns the Claude Code CLI with an explicit argument list, asks for a JSON envelope back, and waits. If things stall, it escalates — a polite termination signal first, then a forced kill if needed.

Here's the part worth knowing: the runner parses the response even when the process exits with an error. That's because refusals show up exactly that way — a failing exit code paired with a well-formed envelope that spells out why.

Whatever comes back, every field gets written to disk. Success or failure, doesn't matter. Along with it, you get the full argument vector, the resolved model, token counts, and how long the whole thing took.
